screens.title: Structured Troubleshooting: Divide and Conquer
screens.narratorSegment: Divide and conquer is a practical method for diagnosing complex systems. The claim is simple: decompose the problem into layers or components and test each one until the failing component is isolated. For example, if a web application is unresponsive, ask whether the client can reach the load balancer, whether the load balancer can reach the EC2 instances, and whether instances can reach the database. By validating network, application, and dependency layers in sequence you either find the fault or eliminate possibilities. A concrete walkthrough: confirm the client's TCP connection to the load balancer; use load balancer health checks to see which backends are marked healthy; SSH or Session Manager into an instance and validate the application process. A common misconception is assuming the most visible layer is the cause — a failing health check might be a misconfigured target rather than a crashed instance. The takeaway is to make your checks small, observable, and reversible. After isolating the fault, ask whether the fix addresses the root cause or merely masks a symptom. Structured Troubleshooting: Divide and Conquer means test each layer to find the real fault and avoid fixes that only hide symptoms.. In practical terms, break systems into testable layers and eliminate healthy components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Divide and Conquer
Definition

Divide and conquer troubleshooting

Split the system into layers and validate each layer to reduce the fault domain quickly.

Why it matters
  • Prevents chasing symptoms by confirming each assumption.
  • Makes diagnostics repeatable and communicable to teams.
  • Helps identify process or configuration errors, not just outages.
Key Takeaway

Validate connectivity, health, and dependencies in small steps; stop when you find a failing test.

Process Flow
1. Network reachability
Can client reach load balancer? Can LB reach instances?
2. Application health
Are processes running and responding to health checks?
3. Dependencies
Are databases and external APIs reachable and healthy?
Concrete example
If a site is slow, first verify load balancer connections and target health. If targets are unhealthy, check instance processes and recent logs before restarting services. This sequence finds whether the issue is networking, application, or dependency related.
Common mistake
Restarting services immediately without collecting logs can hide the root cause and make post-incident analysis harder.
Check your understanding
Can you list three observable checks you would run before rebooting an instance?

screens.title: The 5 Whys Technique
screens.narratorSegment: The 5 Whys is a deliberate interrogation: keep asking "Why?" until you reach a root cause that leads to a systemic change. It’s not always five questions, but the discipline matters. For example: the website is slow — why? The database is overloaded. Why? A new query is inefficient. Why? It lacks an index. Why? Developers were not aware of the indexing requirement. Why? Documentation and code review neglected the data model. This sequence shows how an incident investigation converts into a process improvement: you fix the index and then change the development checklist to prevent recurrence. A common misconception is treating 5 Whys as a blame tool; instead use it to identify process gaps and training needs. During incidents, use 5 Whys after you stabilize the system and have gathered logs and metrics so your questions refer to facts, not guesses. The practical goal is to produce one durable remediation and one preventive change after each incident. The 5 Whys Technique means use repeated 'why' questioning to move from immediate fixes to durable process improvements.. In practical terms, peel back symptomatic layers to find process and human causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › AWS CLI & SDKs
Purpose

Quick, scriptable state collection

Use the CLI for repeatable queries and SDKs to embed checks into automation and runbooks.

Practice tip
Save typical describe and get-metric commands as incident snippets. Log their outputs for post-incident review.
Common misconception
CLI is not riskier than the console; it becomes safer when commands are scripted, logged, and peer-reviewed.
Examples
# Check status of an EC2 instance
aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids i-0abcdef1234567890

# Get CloudWatch metrics for an Application Load Balancer
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB \
  --metric-name HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/my-elb/abcdef123 \
  --start-time 2023-10-27T10:00:00Z \
  --end-time 2023-10-27T10:30:00Z \
  --period 60 \
  --statistic Sum
Capture the JSON output and include timestamps in your incident log. These snippets are safe to run for read-only inspection.
Key Takeaway

Make CLI checks part of your incident playbook and log their outputs for auditability.

screens.title: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Session Manager provides secure shell access to EC2 instances without the operational overhead of SSH keys and bastion hosts. The key benefits are twofold: no inbound port exposure and built-in session logging. Remember to ensure IAM instance profile permissions and SSM Agent health before relying on Session Manager in an incident. This tool reduces blast radius and simplifies secure operations in production. Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Session Manager
Definition

Session Manager overview

A method to access EC2 shells through the SSM Agent, without SSH keys or open inbound ports.

Why use it
  • No inbound port exposure or bastions.
  • All sessions can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for auditability.
  • Simpler permission model via IAM instance profiles.
Start a session (example)
aws ssm start-session --target i-0abcdef1234567890
Ensure the instance role includes AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore and the SSM Agent is running.
Key Takeaway

Use Session Manager for auditable, port-free access in production incidents.

Instance diagnostics
Once connected, common commands include top, htop, dmesg, journalctl, netstat, and lsof for process and network diagnostics. Collect outputs to logs before making changes.
Common misconception
Session Manager is not a debugging magic wand; it requires agent health and correct IAM role configuration to work reliably.
Check your setup
  • SSM Agent running on the instance.
  • Instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  • CloudWatch or S3 configured for session logs if audit is required.

screens.title: Instance Diagnostics: Commands to Know
screens.narratorSegment: When you're inside an instance, a handful of familiar Linux tools give immediate insight into system health. The printout of the top command shows C P U and memory consumers; df -h reports disk usage which can reveal a full partition causing process failures. Netstat or socket listings show listening ports and established connections; lsof reveals which process holds a file or socket open. Dmesg and journalctl surface kernel and system messages that explain crashes or OOM events. Use these tools to form hypotheses: if top shows a runaway process, gather its logs and consider a graceful restart; if df -h shows a full /var partition, free space before restarting services. A common error is running destructive commands like rm -rf without backups; always collect evidence first. After you collect outputs, attach them to your incident timeline and correlate with CloudWatch metrics and Flow Logs. The practical pattern is observe, capture, and then act with minimal scope. In practical terms, top, df -h, netstat, lsof and how they guide your next step. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Instance Diagnostics

Common diagnostic commands

top / htop
CPU and memory consumers; sort by usage to find hot processes.
df -h
Disk usage by filesystem; full partitions often break services.
netstat / ss
Active sockets and listening ports; useful to confirm service bindings.
lsof
Identify which process holds files or sockets open.
Example workflow
If you see high CPU in top, note the process ID, collect its logs with a timestamp, check open sockets with lsof, and inspect recent kernel messages with dmesg for OOM or hardware errors before restarting it.
Safety reminder
Avoid destructive commands until you have backups or redundancy. When in doubt, collect data and consult the incident checklist.
Key Takeaway

Use diagnostic tools to form evidence-backed actions; then perform minimal, auditable changes.

screens.title: Network Troubleshooting Components
screens.narratorSegment: Network issues in AWS often come from a configuration mismatch between Security Groups, Network ACLs, or a missing route. Security Groups are stateful, instance-level virtual firewalls; if an inbound rule is missing, traffic to the instance will be blocked, but return traffic is allowed for permitted connections. Network ACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet level; an explicit deny in a network ACL can block traffic even if security group rules allow it. Route Tables control where traffic is sent within the VPC and to external gateways; a missing route to a NAT gateway or peering connection will prevent reachability. VPC Flow Logs provide observability: they capture information about IP traffic to and from network interfaces and are essential when you need to confirm REJECT actions or find the source IPs affected. A common pitfall is changing security group rules without checking NACLs or route tables. The practical pattern is: verify security groups, then NACLs, then routes, and use flow logs to confirm whether traffic is being rejected or never routed. In practical terms, security groups, network acls, route tables, and vpc flow logs explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Network Troubleshooting
Security Groups
Stateful, instance-level firewalls. Ensure inbound and outbound rules permit intended ports and sources.
Network ACLs
Stateless, subnet-level rules. Explicit denies override permissive security group assumptions.
Route Tables
Define where traffic flows. Missing routes to gateways block connectivity even when security groups permit it.
VPC Flow Logs
Flow logs capture IP traffic metadata for ENIs. They help you find REJECT actions and identify source and destination IPs that experienced blocked traffic.
Practical sequence: confirm security group rules first, then network ACLs, then route tables. If traffic is still failing, run a Flow Log query to find rejects and confirm whether the packet reached the VPC boundary.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch Logs Insights
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs record metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces and are essential when you need to know whether traffic was rejected or simply never routed. By publishing flow logs to CloudWatch Logs, you can run Logs Insights queries to find REJECT entries and identify source IPs and ports quickly. A practical query filters for logStatus equals OK and action equals REJECT, sorts by timestamp, and limits results to the most recent entries. For example, searching for REJECT records to your EC2 private IP on port 80 will show whether the security group or NACL blocked the traffic. One pitfall is forgetting to enable flow logs on the relevant VPC or subnet; another is interpreting flow logs without correlating timestamps against application logs. Always align the timestamps in your flow log query with the incident window and confirm the srcAddr shown in the results. This gives you conclusive evidence to proceed with a remediation such as updating a security group rule. VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch Logs Insights means query flow logs for reject entries to identify blocked traffic and the responsible network control.. In practical terms, query flow logs to find rejected traffic and confirm sources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › VPC Flow Logs
Why flow logs
They provide recorded evidence of network traffic and the actions applied, which is essential for identifying blocked or rejected traffic during an incident.
Example Logs Insights query
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter logStatus = "OK" and action = "REJECT"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 20
Replace filtering fields with dstAddr or dstPort to narrow results to the instance and service you care about.
Practical steps
  1. Ensure flow logs are enabled for the VPC or subnet and targeting CloudWatch Logs.
  2. Run a Logs Insights query for REJECT actions in the incident time window.
  3. Correlate srcAddr and dstAddr with your client and instance IPs to find the blocker.
Misconception
Flow logs do not show packet payloads; they show metadata. Use them to prove presence and action, then use instance logs for payload-level investigation.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Diagnose Connectivity with Flow Logs & Session Manager
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through a realistic connectivity incident. Start with prerequisites: a running EC2 instance in a public subnet with SSM Agent installed, an IAM instance profile that includes AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, and a VPC Flow Log publishing to CloudWatch Logs. Step one is to verify Session Manager access; start a session and run ping to confirm outbound connectivity. Step two is to simulate a network block by removing an inbound HTTP or HTTPS rule from the instance's Security Group. From outside, try curl to the instance and observe failure. Step three is diagnosis: open CloudWatch Logs Insights on the VPC Flow Logs group and run a REJECT filter for the instance private IP; you should see entries showing your client IP as srcAddr and action equal REJECT. This confirms the security group change blocked traffic. Remediation is step four: re-add the inbound rule and verify curl succeeds. Throughout, capture timestamps, CLI outputs, and flow log results to the incident log so the remediation is auditable. This activity practices safe simulation and evidence-based fixes. Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Lab Walkthrough

Diagnose Network Connectivity — Activity

Prerequisites
  • EC2 with SSM Agent and an instance profile (AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore)
  • VPC Flow Logs enabled to CloudWatch Logs

Safety
Simulate a block in a test environment or during maintenance windows; capture evidence before remediation.
Steps

  2. Remove inbound HTTP/HTTPS rule from the instance Security Group and attempt curl http://<EC2-Public-IP> from your client.

Perform simulated blocks in controlled environments, use Session Manager and Flow Logs to gather proof, and always document timestamps and outputs for post-incident review.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are predictable mistakes that slow incidents and increase risk. The first is symptom-chasing: changing a setting that makes an alert quiet without finding the root cause. For instance, restarting a process might temporarily restore service but hide the underlying inefficiency that will recur. Second, skipping simple checks wastes time — always verify whether the instance is running, whether health checks are failing, and whether a security group rule changed. Third, performing destructive commands without backups or redundancy can make recovery harder. Safety practices address these mistakes: capture evidence first, use Session Manager for auditable access, respect change management for production fixes, and prefer minimal, reversible changes. Maintain incident logs with timestamps, command outputs, and flow log evidence. A final practical tip: when you patch or change configuration, confirm the fix with both functional tests and your earlier evidence artifacts so you can confidently record a durable remediation rather than a stopgap. In practical terms, avoid symptom-chasing and unsafe remediation in production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Troubleshooting in cloud environments is both an intellectual process and a practical skill. In this lesson you will learn how systematic methods like “divide and conquer” and the “5 Whys” direct your investigation so you avoid chasing symptoms. You will also gain familiarity with the most useful AWS tools for incidents: the CLI and SDKs for quick inspection, Systems Manager Session Manager for secure, auditable shell access without opening ports, and VPC Flow Logs plus CloudWatch Logs Insights to confirm whether traffic is being rejected. Practical examples will walk through common scenarios such as an unresponsive web application and a blocked HTTP port. You will also practice safe change management: verify state before you change it, avoid risky commands in production, and prefer auditable actions. By the end of this chapter you’ll have a repeatable mental checklist that reduces time-to-diagnosis and leads to durable fixes rather than temporary workarounds. Where will you apply this checklist first in your environment?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply structured troubleshooting methodologies to diagnose complex system issues with confidence. That means you will practice breaking a problem into smaller components and eliminating healthy services until a root cause appears. You will also use the AWS CLI and SDKs to gather exact state quickly and script those checks so they are reproducible. Next, you'll learn how Systems Manager Session Manager gives secure, auditable access to instances without opening SSH ports, and you will perform live checks using standard Linux diagnostics. Finally, you'll employ network troubleshooting tools: review Security Groups, Network ACLs, Route Tables, and query VPC Flow Logs to find rejected traffic. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters: faster diagnosis, safer access, and evidence-based fixes. Think of these objectives as a competency map: inspect, isolate, verify, and remediate with auditability in every step.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical habits you will form while troubleshooting. You will learn which quick checks to run first so you don’t waste time. For example, confirming that an instance is running or that a load balancer health check is passing often resolves many incidents. You will also learn to collect evidence using CloudWatch metrics and VPC Flow Logs queries so decisions are data-driven instead of speculative. Another objective is building short CLI scripts or SDK calls to reproduce checks, which saves time during recurring incidents. Finally, we emphasize safety: follow change management, avoid destructive commands when uncertain, and prefer session-based access that is automatically logged. These habits reduce risk and support post-incident learning. As you practice, aim to make your first three checks repeatable and quick to run under stress.

Divide and conquer is a practical method for diagnosing complex systems. The claim is simple: decompose the problem into layers or components and test each one until the failing component is isolated. For example, if a web application is unresponsive, ask whether the client can reach the load balancer, whether the load balancer can reach the EC2 instances, and whether instances can reach the database. By validating network, application, and dependency layers in sequence you either find the fault or eliminate possibilities. A concrete walkthrough: confirm the client's TCP connection to the load balancer; use load balancer health checks to see which backends are marked healthy; SSH or Session Manager into an instance and validate the application process. A common misconception is assuming the most visible layer is the cause — a failing health check might be a misconfigured target rather than a crashed instance. The takeaway is to make your checks small, observable, and reversible. After isolating the fault, ask whether the fix addresses the root cause or merely masks a symptom. Structured Troubleshooting: Divide and Conquer means test each layer to find the real fault and avoid fixes that only hide symptoms.. In practical terms, break systems into testable layers and eliminate healthy components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The 5 Whys is a deliberate interrogation: keep asking "Why?" until you reach a root cause that leads to a systemic change. It’s not always five questions, but the discipline matters. For example: the website is slow — why? The database is overloaded. Why? A new query is inefficient. Why? It lacks an index. Why? Developers were not aware of the indexing requirement. Why? Documentation and code review neglected the data model. This sequence shows how an incident investigation converts into a process improvement: you fix the index and then change the development checklist to prevent recurrence. A common misconception is treating 5 Whys as a blame tool; instead use it to identify process gaps and training needs. During incidents, use 5 Whys after you stabilize the system and have gathered logs and metrics so your questions refer to facts, not guesses. The practical goal is to produce one durable remediation and one preventive change after each incident. The 5 Whys Technique means use repeated 'why' questioning to move from immediate fixes to durable process improvements.. In practical terms, peel back symptomatic layers to find process and human causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The AWS CLI and SDKs are your fastest path to consistent, repeatable information during an incident. Rather than navigating the console, a single CLI command can return the exact state you need and be copied into runbooks or chat. For example, use a command to describe an EC2 instance status or to retrieve CloudWatch metrics for a load balancer. These commands are scriptable, so you can build small checks that run the same way each time. A concrete example: when you suspect an instance problem, run the describe-instance-status command to see instance status checks and recent events. For a load balancer, query HTTP 5xx metrics over a time window to detect spikes. A common misconception is that the console is always safer; while the console is useful, the CLI is faster and auditable when output is logged. Practice formatting and saving CLI output in your incident logs so your team can reproduce the same checks later. The goal is reliable, repeatable inspection, not ad-hoc exploration. AWS CLI and SDKs for Rapid Inspection means use cli commands and sdk calls to collect auditable, repeatable state for diagnosis.. In practical terms, gather resource state and metrics quickly using scriptable commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This screen walks through two concrete CLI checks you will use frequently. First, describe-instance-status gives instance status checks and recent events that indicate scheduling, reboot, or underlying hardware issues. Running it with an instance ID quickly tells you whether the instance's system and instance status checks are passing. Second, get-metric-statistics for a load balancer lets you retrieve HTTP 5xx counts over a time range. That metric reveals whether back-end errors are increasing and at what times. The command examples here are read-only and can be logged. A useful practice is to set start and end times relative to the incident window and use a sixty-second period for per-minute granularity. A common mistake is interpreting a single metric spike as the whole story; correlate metrics with logs and instance statuses. After gathering these outputs, attach them to the incident timeline and continue to the next verification step: process and dependency checks inside the instance. CLI Examples: EC2 Status and CloudWatch Metrics means combine ec2 status and cloudwatch metrics with logs to build an evidence-backed timeline.. When you're inside an instance, a handful of familiar Linux tools give immediate insight into system health. The printout of the top command shows C P U and memory consumers; df -h reports disk usage which can reveal a full partition causing process failures. Netstat or socket listings show listening ports and established connections; lsof reveals which process holds a file or socket open. Dmesg and journalctl surface kernel and system messages that explain crashes or OOM events. Use these tools to form hypotheses: if top shows a runaway process, gather its logs and consider a graceful restart; if df -h shows a full /var partition, free space before restarting services. A common error is running destructive commands like rm -rf without backups; always collect evidence first. Network issues in AWS often come from a configuration mismatch between Security Groups, Network ACLs, or a missing route. Security Groups are stateful, instance-level virtual firewalls; if an inbound rule is missing, traffic to the instance will be blocked, but return traffic is allowed for permitted connections. Network ACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet level; an explicit deny in a network ACL can block traffic even if security group rules allow it. Route Tables control where traffic is sent within the VPC and to external gateways; a missing route to a NAT gateway or peering connection will prevent reachability. VPC Flow Logs provide observability: they capture information about IP traffic to and from network interfaces and are essential when you need to confirm REJECT actions or find the source IPs affected. A common pitfall is changing security group rules without checking NACLs or route tables. The practical pattern is: verify security groups, then NACLs, then routes, and use flow logs to confirm whether traffic is being rejected or never routed. There are predictable mistakes that slow incidents and increase risk. The first is symptom-chasing: changing a setting that makes an alert quiet without finding the root cause. For instance, restarting a process might temporarily restore service but hide the underlying inefficiency that will recur. Second, skipping simple checks wastes time — always verify whether the instance is running, whether health checks are failing, and whether a security group rule changed. Third, performing destructive commands without backups or redundancy can make recovery harder. Safety practices address these mistakes: capture evidence first, use Session Manager for auditable access, respect change management for production fixes, and prefer minimal, reversible changes. Maintain incident logs with timestamps, command outputs, and flow log evidence.
